walters:48.2667.summary: This small disc of fired clay is pressed with a worn image of the Virgin enthroned, holding the Christ Child on her lap, between two flanking figures, perhaps angels, under a raised border. As its museum title indicates, it is a pilgrim's token, a humble keepsake carried home from a journey to a holy place.
facts: The Walters bought the token from Simon Bendall, London, in 1991, and attributes it to Syria.
walters:48.2667.notes: Identification uncertain only in detail: the Virgin's seated figure is clear in the old black-and-white photograph, but the Child is barely legible. Date 6th–7th century per museum.

feat:maskell-ivory-crucifixion.summary: On a small ivory panel from a casket of Passion scenes, Christ hangs on the cross, alive, upright and open-eyed, beneath the inscription REX IVD[AEORUM], 'King of the Jews', while the Virgin, Saint John and the soldier with the spear stand nearby. To the left, Judas hangs lifeless from a tree, his bag of silver spilled at his feet. Together with the doors of Santa Sabina, it is among the very earliest surviving narrative images of the Crucifixion, and its contrast of the two deaths, one defeated and one triumphant, is a profound meditation on the cross.
facts: The panel is one of four from the same casket, which together show Pilate washing his hands, Peter's denial, Christ carrying the cross, the Crucifixion, the empty tomb and Thomas touching the wounds.
Christ is shown not slumped in suffering but heroically alive, with a strong, athletic body, a way of showing victory over death that would dominate Crucifixion images for centuries.
The panels are known as the 'Maskell Ivories' after William Maskell, the collector and writer on ivories from whom the British Museum acquired them in the nineteenth century.
The tree from which Judas hangs bears a bird feeding its young, often read as a sign of the new life that springs from Christ's death.

feat:gregorio-fernandez-cristo-yacente.summary: The dead Christ lies on a white shroud, his head resting on a pillow, the wounds of the Passion rendered with almost unbearable tenderness and realism. Gregorio Fernández, the leading sculptor of Castile, created a series of these recumbent Christs for meditation and Holy Week devotion, and this example — made for the Jesuit professed house in Madrid — is among the finest. It embodies the Counter-Reformation ideal of art that moves the faithful to compassion and prayer.
facts: Fernández heightened realism with 'postizos' — added materials such as glass eyes, ivory teeth and fingernails, cork for clotted blood, and resin for drops of sweat and tears.
The polychromy (painting) was a separate specialized craft; this figure's pale, luminous flesh tones were painted by Jerónimo de Calabria.
Even the sheet and pillow are carved in wood, the pillow painted to imitate embroidery; the sculpture passed to the Spanish state after the Jesuits were expelled in 1767.

The format of Christ laid out alone, as if in the tomb, became one of the most widespread devotional images in Spain, and Fernández's model was repeated by his workshop and followers for many churches and convents.
